content.title: About
content.content: Nonfat cereals and granola bars are dry grain products made without added fats. They typically contain whole grains, bran, dried fruit, sweeteners, and added vitamins and minerals for enrichment. The product is aimed at people who monitor fat intake but still want energy and nutrients from grains.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Nonfat cereals are popular in sports nutrition because they are quickly digested and provide rapid energy.
Fat‑free granola bars may contain more sugar to compensate for the lack of flavor, so checking the ingredient list is important.
The “fat‑free” process usually removes oil from the grains and replaces it with dry ingredients rather than eliminating all lipids.
In many countries these products must be labeled as “low‑calorie” or “low‑fat.”
Fiber content in nonfat cereals is often higher than in their full‑fat counterparts due to the use of bran.

items.title: Rich in complex carbohydrates
items.content: Complex carbs provide sustained satiety and a stable blood‑glucose level.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B2, B3 and folate support metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, helps normalize cholesterol, and supports gut microbiota.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Suitable for low‑fat diets and for individuals controlling calorie intake.

items.title: Fortified with minerals
items.content: Often enriched with iron, zinc and magnesium, which are essential for blood formation and muscle function.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: To replace flavor lost without fat, many products add significant amounts of sugar or syrups, raising the glycemic index.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: The product may contain nuts, soy protein, gluten, or dried fruit—check the label if you have allergies.

items.title: Lack of healthy fats
items.content: Absence of fats can reduce absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), which should be obtained from other sources.

items.title: Potential additives
items.content: Some versions contain artificial sweeteners, flavors or preservatives that may be undesirable for sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cereals can be poured over milk, kefir or plant‑based drinks and topped with fresh berries. Granola bars are convenient for on‑the‑go snacks; they can be broken up and added to yogurt or oatmeal.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in a sealed package. After opening, keep the product in an airtight container to prevent moisture absorption and loss of crunch.

content.title: About
content.content: Instant coffee, decaffeinated, reconstituted (5206) is a dry powder made from roasted coffee beans that have had the caffeine removed and then dried by freeze‑drying or spray‑drying. When mixed with hot water it dissolves into a flavorful beverage without the stimulating effect of caffeine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Caffeine removal often uses supercritical CO₂ or water‑based processes, preserving most flavor compounds.
Instant coffee takes up less space and is easier to transport than ground or whole bean coffee.
Reconstituted coffee can be prepared instantly by adding hot water, making it convenient for travel or office use.
The powder retains a large portion of the antioxidants found in regular coffee, though in slightly lower amounts.
Decaffeinated coffee is popular among people sensitive to caffeine or those who experience insomnia.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Even after decaffeination, the product still holds polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports metabolism
items.content: Certain coffee compounds may aid metabolic rate and help regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: May lower risk of some diseases
items.content: Regular moderate consumption of decaf coffee is linked to a reduced risk of type 2 diabetes and some cancers.

items.title: Improves digestion
items.content: Coffee stimulates gastric secretions, which can aid digestion without the nervous stimulation of caffeine.

items.title: Hydration contribution
items.content: Decaf instant coffee adds to daily fluid intake, especially when consumed without added sugar.

items.title: Coffee allergy
items.content: A minority of individuals may experience allergic reactions to coffee components, manifesting as skin rashes or gastrointestinal symptoms.

items.title: Additive content
items.content: Some brands add flavorings, sweeteners, or preservatives that may not be suitable for sensitive consumers.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Even without caffeine, coffee remains acidic and can irritate the stomach lining if consumed in excess.

items.title: Possible solvent residues
items.content: Chemical decaffeination methods can leave trace solvent residues; choose products with proper certification.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: For a 200 ml cup, dissolve 1–2 g (about 1 teaspoon) of powder in hot water (90‑95 °C). Add milk, a plant‑based alternative, or a sweetener if desired. The powder dissolves quickly without leaving sediment.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the lid tightly sealed to prevent moisture absorption. Discard the product if it develops a moldy odor or off‑taste.

potato-roasted-from-fresh-peel-eaten-fat.title: Potato, roasted, from fresh, peel eaten, fat added

content.title: About
content.content: Roasted potato made from fresh tubers is diced or sliced potato that is either peeled or left with skin, then fried in oil until golden and crisp. The skin may be kept when edible, preserving extra nutrients. Frying gives the dish its characteristic aroma and crunchy texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potato is one of the most widely consumed vegetables worldwide.
Frying in oil increases calorie content but enhances flavor and aroma.
The skin is rich in fiber, vitamin C, vitamin K, and polyphenols.
Traditionally roasted potatoes are cooked in vegetable oil, but butter or olive oil can be used.
In many cultures roasted potatoes are served as a side, snack, or main dish.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Potatoes provide carbohydrates that quickly convert to glucose, supplying the body with energy.

items.title: High in fiber (when skin is kept)
items.content: The skin contains dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion and satiety.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Potatoes contain vitamin C, vitamin B6, potassium and magnesium, important for nerve and muscle function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Polysaccharides and phenolic compounds in the skin have antioxidant activity.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure, and moderate amounts of healthy fats from the oil can improve lipid profiles.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Frying adds a significant amount of fat, so portion control is important, especially on weight‑loss diets.

items.title: Trans fats from improper oil use
items.content: Repeated heating of vegetable oils can create trans fats, which are harmful to heart health.

items.title: Allergy to certain fats
items.content: Some individuals may be intolerant or allergic to specific fats such as butter.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: High‑temperature frying can produce acrylamide, a potential carcinogen; avoid over‑cooking.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Roasted potatoes are served hot as a side dish, in wedges, slices or cubes. They can be seasoned with salt, spices, herbs or cheese. Keeping the skin adds texture and nutrients. Pair them with salads or protein‑rich foods for a balanced meal.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked roasted potatoes in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat in the oven or skillet to restore crispness. Do not leave at room temperature for more than 2 hours to prevent bacterial growth.

content.title: About
content.content: Spam reduced sodium is a canned meat product made from pork, beef and chicken with a lower salt content. It has a soft texture, a mild smoky flavor and is convenient for quick meal preparation.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The original Spam was introduced in 1937 by Hormel Foods.
The reduced‑sodium version appeared in the early 2000s in response to growing health concerns.
Spam is a staple in military rations because of its long shelf life.
It has become a popular ingredient in Hawaiian and Japanese cuisine.
One can contains roughly 300 kcal.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: A 100‑g serving provides about 13 g of high‑quality animal protein, essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Reduced sodium
items.content: Compared with regular Spam, the sodium content is cut by almost half, making it more suitable for those monitoring salt intake.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Spam contains thiamine, niacin and vitamin B12, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Convenient and long‑lasting
items.content: The canned product can be stored for up to 5 years without refrigeration, ideal for emergency supplies.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Spam contains about 15 g of fat per 100 g, including saturated fat, so it should be eaten in moderation.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to pork or beef may experience reactions.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: The product includes nitrites and other preservatives that some people may wish to avoid.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice and fry Spam, add it to omelets, salads, sandwiches, or use it in Asian‑style dishes such as fried rice with vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the product refrigerated in a sealed container and consume within 5 days.
